challenge.better_approach: Considered: git LFS for the journal (adds a service dependency; GitHub is hosting-only per the project), and gzip of old lines (still one growing file). A rotation that keeps the head's path is the smallest change: the path readers (inspector.py, tester red_tickets.py and hollow.py, cc prove.sh and close.sh, the installer) and the merge driver all address the head.
challenge.hidden_assumption: That nothing reads the whole journal by path. The path readers above may replay it themselves rather than calling read_journal; the build must census them (grep for .artifact-journal) and route any whole-file reader through read_journal, or the cut hides old entries from it.
challenge.prior_art: In house: ticket 0f8aefbba1d0 (a journal line lands at the path even when git replaced it) and the journal merge driver b7d2e05a1c93 both assume one file; the orchestrator grepped the corpus and found no journal size or rotation ticket. In the field, this is log rotation with a hash-chained ledger: the seal carries the last hash forward, as in Certificate Transparency's tree heads.
challenge.real_collision: None real. The merge driver merges the head and would be unchanged. A sealed segment is immutable, so two boxes splitting at different points would collide; that is a distinction the build must settle (split at a deterministic entry count, not on the local file size).

answers.falsifier: A scratch journal past the bound is split into a sealed segment plus a head, each under the bound, and verify_chain over the root returns no faults. Editing one byte of the sealed segment, or the head's first prev, makes verify_chain name the fault at the seam. The live journal on a box past the bound is split on its next append, and the push carries no GH001 warning.
answers.from_idea: none, because this was measured, not imagined: the GitHub GH001 large-file warning on the Dell push of cairn/.artifact-journal.jsonl at 50.04 MB (relayed by the orchestrator 2026-11-15; 33 MB, 22895 lines on akiendelllinux the same day), owned by cairn/tools/artifact/artifact.py
answers.how: The journal at a root becomes segmented. The head stays at .artifact-journal.jsonl, so every appender and path reader keeps working. When the head passes a byte bound, artifact seals it into .artifact-journal/<NNNN>.jsonl, and the new head's first entry chains prev to the sealed segment's last entry sha. read_journal and verify_chain read the sealed segments in order, then the head. A red-first proof in cairn/tools/artifact/proofs builds a scratch root over the bound and shows the chain replays whole across the cut, and that a broken link at the seam is named.
answers.traces_to: Law 7 (errors are permanent in records of truth): the journal is the who/when record of every record write, and a push GitHub refuses at 100 MB loses it. Law 4: the bound is enforced by the door that appends, not by remembering to trim.
answers.what: cairn's artifact journal stays under GitHub's per-file limits as it grows, with verify_chain still replaying one unbroken chain from genesis.

bullets.text: cairn/.artifact-journal.jsonl: 50.04 MB on the Dell push (GH001 warns at 50 MB, refuses at 100 MB); 33 MB, 22895 lines here.
Split at a deterministic entry count so every box seals the same segment bytes; a size-based cut would fork the segments across boxes.

title: cairn's artifact journal stays under GitHub's per-file limits as it grows, with verify_chain still replaying one unbroke
